extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy; theorists and policymakers interested in natural rights, property, and family authority
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting Locke's normative criteria about when slavery is legitimate, how property is acquired and limited, the role of labour and money, and the nature and limits of parental power. Useful for analysis of natural-rights property theory and familial authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions of legitimate slavery
rubrics_metrics.description: Slavery is the 'state of war continued, between a lawful conqueror and a captive'; it is only legitimate when a person has forfeited his life by some fault that deserves death, so that the conqueror may lawfully detain or use him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A man cannot, by compact or consent, enslave himself to another or grant absolute arbitrary power over his life; only forfeiture by just desert (an act deserving death) can justify one being kept in slavery. If a compact limits the conqueror’s power, the state of war and slavery ceases while the compact endures. Historical practices of selling persons among Jews and others were to drudgery (temporary service), not absolute slavery, because masters lacked arbitrary power to kill or maim at pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: God gave the world in common
rubrics_metrics.description: Locke asserts God gave the earth 'to the children of men... to mankind in common.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This premise raises the question how private property arises absent universal consent; Locke uses it as the starting point for deriving appropriation rights through labour rather than as a justification for exclusive dominion by one person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labour-mixing theory of property
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever a person removes from the common state of nature and mixes his labour with becomes his property: 'The labour of his body, and the work of his hands... makes it his property.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: gathering acorns, hunting a deer, drawing water into a pitcher — the act of labour distinguishes those items from the common and annexes them to the labourer. This holds 'at least where there is enough, and as good, left in common for others.' Labour is the 'unquestionable property of the labourer' and thereby grounds his exclusive right to what his labour joins to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation begins at gathering/first taking
rubrics_metrics.description: The moment of first gathering or taking from nature (e.g., picking acorns) is when appropriation begins: 'if the first gathering made them not his, nothing else could.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No universal consent of all commoners is required for initial appropriation; requiring such consent would make appropriation impossible and lead to starvation. Practical illustrations (pitcher, turf, ore dug) show appropriation by labour without assignation from others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit of appropriation — enough and as good left
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of nature bounds property: one may appropriate 'as much as any one can make use of to any advantage of life before it spoils' and no more; anything beyond use that spoils is more than his share and belongs to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriation must leave 'enough, and as good' for others; hoarding perishables beyond use is theft and violates natural law. The spoilage limit is the key restraint on initial appropriation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement and enclosure confer title to land
rubrics_metrics.description: Property in land arises when a person tills, plants, improves, cultivates, and can use the product of the land; 'by his labour' he incloses it from the common and annexes his labour to it making it his property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivation and subduing the earth are tied to dominion; labour complying with God's command to subdue the earth gives title. Early societies later formalize these titles by positive law and compact, but the original title derives from improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of property by labour and conveniencies of life
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature's measure of legitimate possession is set by the extent of a man's labour and the conveniencies of life: 'no man's labour could subdue, or appropriate all; nor could his enjoyment consume more than a small part...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possessions should be moderate and limited to what one can use without injuring others; in early ages, this measure sufficed to prevent quarrels. Labour and usable convenience, not mere size of dominion, determine just property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spoilage as a moral constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: If goods (fruits, venison, produce) perish in a possessor's hands unused, he has offended the common law of nature and may be punished; he 'invaded his neighbour’s share' by keeping more than he could use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enforces the spoilage limit: the wrongness lies not in having much per se but in letting durable commons that could benefit others be wasted through hoarding perishable goods beyond need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labour creates value — labour as principal source of value
rubrics_metrics.description: Labour puts the difference of value on things; 'the improvement of labour makes the far greater part of the value' and 'in most of them ninety-nine hundredths are wholly to be put on the account of labour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke supports this with examples tracing all the labour inputs behind common commodities (bread, cloth) and uses it to justify why improvement and industry legitimately produce private wealth and raise the common stock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement increases the common stock
rubrics_metrics.description: By cultivating and improving land a person 'gives ninety acres to mankind' because improved land yields far more produce than waste land; enclosure and industry increase overall provision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used to defend appropriation: appropriation by labour does not impoverish others but augments the productive capacity available to mankind (thus reconciles private property with common good).

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction of durable money alters appropriation limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention and consent to use money (gold and silver) allows men to hoard value without spoiling, enabling accumulation beyond what one can personally use and permitting unequal possession of land by exchanging perishable goods for durable money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Money's durability and agreed value remove the spoilage constraint and permit people to rightfully possess more land than they personally use; such unequal possessions arise by tacit consent and are regulated by governments and positive law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customs and civil law can restrict appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where land is common by compact (e.g., English commons) and people live under government, one cannot appropriate without the consent of fellow-commoners; property and possession are ultimately determined by positive constitutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke distinguishes the original natural rules from later civil arrangements: positive law can create or restrict rights of enclosure and property by social compact and the law of the land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental (paternal) power is temporary and shared
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents (both father and mother) have a temporary power or jurisdiction over their children to preserve, nourish, and educate them until they reach the use of reason; this is not an absolute dominion but a provisional guardianship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke criticizes the term 'paternal power' for obscuring the mother's equal role and emphasizes scriptural and natural grounds for parental authority. The bonds of subjection loosen as age and reason mature, until children attain natural equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children are not under the law of reason until they can use reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Because law presupposes the capacity to understand it, infants who lack use of reason are not yet under the law of reason and thus require parental governance to secure their general good and protect them from harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parental authority is justified as necessary care until the child can be directed by reason itself; once capable, the person is under natural law and entitled to freedom equal to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural equality in jurisdiction — limits on arbitrary dominion
rubrics_metrics.description: All men are equal in respect of 'jurisdiction or dominion one over another' — natural equality means no one has arbitrary authority over others by birth; distinctions of age, virtue, or merit may give precedent but not absolute dominion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equality underpins objections to hereditary absolute monarchy and to paternal absolutism; any special authority must be justified by reason, benefit, or temporary necessity rather than natural permanent dominion.
